frames.narration: The broadcaster's encoder pushes 1080p video over SRT to the ingest gateway nearest to them, with a stream key. The gateway checks the key before accepting any media.

The gateway writes the raw stream into the buffer, and a transcoder reads it. It produces four renditions, 1080p at 6,000, 720p at 3,000, 480p at 1,200 and 240p at 400 kbit/s, all cut at the same two-second keyframe boundaries.
The packager wraps each finished rendition into segments and parts and updates the playlist. Segment 1042 is written to the origin store in all four renditions.
A viewer's player asks its nearest CDN edge for the 720p version of segment 1042, chosen because its last downloads measured about 4 Mbit/s. This edge has not got the segment yet.

The shield has not got it either, so it goes to the origin once. The 40,000 other viewers who ask for the same segment in the same moment wait for that one answer instead of sending their own, which is request coalescing.
The segment flows back through the edge to the player and stays cached at both tiers. Everybody who joins this city later gets it from the edge in a few milliseconds.

With two-second segments and a hold-back of three segments, this viewer is about 9.2 seconds behind the camera. With half-second parts and a hold-back of three parts, the same pipeline gives about 3.2 seconds, but the player makes four times as many requests.

The ingest gateway then fails. The encoder reconnects to the standby with the same stream key, and the packager resumes at the next segment boundary. A viewer who holds three segments of buffer never notices a gap of a few seconds.
